callouts.label: RNA primer (leading strand)
callouts.hint: Short red segment at the very start (5' end) of the new leading strand, near the fork origin in the upper-center area.
callouts.description: The RNA primer on the leading strand is a short stretch of RNA (about 10 nucleotides) synthesized by primase. It provides the free 3'-OH group that DNA Polymerase III requires to begin adding DNA nucleotides. The leading strand needs only one RNA primer for its entire length because synthesis is continuous. Later, DNA Polymerase I removes this primer and replaces it with DNA.
callouts.ap_tip: A critical AP concept: DNA polymerase CANNOT start a new strand from scratch — it can only ADD nucleotides to an existing 3'-OH group. This is why primase must first lay down an RNA primer. This limitation of DNA polymerase is fundamental to understanding why primers are needed and why replication cannot begin without primase.

callouts.label: Single-strand binding proteins (SSB)
callouts.hint: Multiple small teal oval/bean-shaped proteins coating the exposed single-stranded DNA regions between helicase and the polymerases, in the center of the image.
callouts.description: Single-strand binding proteins (SSBs) bind cooperatively to the exposed single-stranded DNA after helicase separates the parental strands. They prevent the single strands from re-annealing (snapping back together) or forming secondary structures like hairpin loops that would block replication. SSBs do not permanently cover the DNA — they are displaced as DNA Polymerase III advances along the template.
callouts.ap_tip: SSB proteins stabilize single-stranded DNA but do NOT participate in base pairing or strand synthesis. The AP exam tests whether students understand the difference between structural support proteins (SSB) and catalytic enzymes (polymerases, helicase). SSBs are sometimes confused with histones — histones package double-stranded DNA, while SSBs stabilize single-stranded DNA.

callouts.label: Topoisomerase
callouts.hint: Small round gold-colored protein sitting on the parental DNA ahead of (to the left of) the fork junction.
callouts.description: Topoisomerase (also called gyrase in prokaryotes) relieves the torsional strain that builds up ahead of the replication fork as helicase unwinds the double helix. It does this by cutting one or both DNA strands, allowing them to swivel and release the supercoiling tension, then resealing the breaks. Without topoisomerase, the DNA ahead of the fork would become overwound and replication would stall.
callouts.ap_tip: Topoisomerase is the target of several antibiotics (like ciprofloxacin) and anticancer drugs (like topotecan). The AP exam may ask why blocking topoisomerase stops cell division — it prevents DNA replication by causing lethal torsional stress ahead of the fork.

callouts.label: Parental DNA double helix
callouts.hint: Two intertwined gray strands with base-pair rungs in the left quarter of the image, before the fork opens.
callouts.description: The parental DNA double helix consists of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands wound around each other in a right-handed helix. The strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs (A-T and G-C). During replication, the helicase enzyme unwinds this helix at the replication fork, separating the two strands so each can serve as a template for a new complementary strand.
callouts.ap_tip: The AP exam frequently tests the semiconservative nature of DNA replication — each daughter molecule contains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesized strand. This was demonstrated by the Meselson-Stahl experiment using heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N). Know this experiment in detail.

callouts.label: Helicase
callouts.hint: Large ring-shaped or wedge-shaped bright blue enzyme at the center of the fork junction where the two strands separate.
callouts.description: Helicase is a ring-shaped enzyme that uses energy from ATP hydrolysis to break the hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs, unwinding the parental double helix at the replication fork. It travels along one strand in the 5'→3' direction, prying the two strands apart and creating single-stranded templates for DNA synthesis. Helicase is one of the first enzymes to act at the replication fork.
callouts.ap_tip: Know that helicase breaks HYDROGEN bonds between base pairs — not the covalent phosphodiester bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone. The AP exam uses this distinction as a common trick question. Also remember: helicase uses ATP energy to unwind DNA.

callouts.label: Primase
callouts.hint: Small orange oval enzyme on the lagging template strand near the fork, shown laying down a new RNA primer.
callouts.description: Primase is an RNA polymerase that synthesizes short RNA primers (about 10 nucleotides) on the lagging strand template. Unlike DNA polymerase, primase CAN start a new nucleic acid strand from scratch without a pre-existing 3'-OH group. On the lagging strand, primase must act repeatedly — each time helicase unwinds a new stretch of template, primase lays down another primer so DNA Pol III can synthesize the next Okazaki fragment.
callouts.ap_tip: Primase is sometimes confused with DNA Polymerase III on the AP exam. Key distinction: primase makes RNA and can START new strands; DNA Pol III makes DNA and can only EXTEND existing strands. Primase works once on the leading strand but many times on the lagging strand.

callouts.label: DNA Polymerase III (leading)
callouts.hint: Large oval forest green enzyme at the growing tip of the new leading strand in the upper right area of the diagram.
callouts.description: DNA Polymerase III is the primary replication enzyme in prokaryotes (in eukaryotes, the equivalent is DNA Polymerase epsilon for the leading strand). It reads the template strand in the 3'→5' direction and synthesizes the new complementary strand in the 5'→3' direction, adding about 1,000 nucleotides per second. It has proofreading ability (3'→5' exonuclease activity) that allows it to remove and replace incorrectly paired nucleotides, achieving an error rate of about 1 in 10 billion base pairs.
callouts.ap_tip: DNA Polymerase III has TWO key activities: (1) 5'→3' polymerase activity (adds nucleotides) and (2) 3'→5' exonuclease proofreading (removes errors). The AP exam tests the direction rule: all DNA polymerases synthesize ONLY in the 5'→3' direction. This is the fundamental constraint that creates the leading/lagging strand asymmetry.

callouts.label: New leading strand
callouts.hint: Continuous bright green strand running from the fork toward the upper right, parallel to the upper template strand.
callouts.description: The new leading strand is synthesized continuously in the 5'→3' direction, which happens to be the same direction as fork movement. Because the template strand runs 3'→5' (the direction DNA Polymerase III reads), synthesis proceeds smoothly toward the fork without interruption. Only one RNA primer is needed, and Pol III extends this single strand as fast as helicase unwinds the DNA.
callouts.ap_tip: The leading strand is synthesized CONTINUOUSLY because its 5'→3' synthesis direction matches the direction of fork opening. The AP exam often asks students to compare leading and lagging strand synthesis — remember that 'leading' means continuous and 'lagging' means discontinuous (Okazaki fragments).

callouts.label: Lagging strand template
callouts.hint: The lower template strand running from the fork toward the lower right, in light gray. Single-stranded where exposed.
callouts.description: The lagging strand template runs in the 5'→3' direction away from the fork. Because DNA Polymerase III can only synthesize in the 5'→3' direction, it must work AWAY from the fork on this template — the opposite direction from fork movement. This means synthesis on the lagging strand is discontinuous: as the fork opens up new template, primase must repeatedly lay down new primers, and Pol III synthesizes short fragments back toward previously replicated DNA.
callouts.ap_tip: The lagging strand template is read 3'→5' by Pol III (same as always), but because this template strand is oriented 5'→3' toward the fork, Pol III must move AWAY from the fork. This antiparallel orientation is the entire reason the lagging strand exists. The AP exam frequently tests this directionality concept.

callouts.label: DNA Polymerase III (lagging)
callouts.hint: Large oval forest green enzyme on the lagging strand, extending the most recent Okazaki fragment nearest the fork.
callouts.description: DNA Polymerase III on the lagging strand performs the same 5'→3' synthesis as on the leading strand, but it must repeatedly dissociate and reassociate with new primers. After completing one Okazaki fragment, Pol III releases the template, moves to the newest RNA primer near the fork, and begins extending the next fragment. In prokaryotes, the leading and lagging strand Pol III enzymes are physically connected through a clamp loader complex, coordinating their activity at the fork.
callouts.ap_tip: The AP exam may show a diagram and ask which direction Pol III moves on each strand. On BOTH strands, Pol III synthesizes 5'→3'. The difference is that on the leading strand this direction follows the fork, while on the lagging strand it moves away from the fork. Same enzyme, same direction, different consequence.

callouts.label: Okazaki fragments
callouts.hint: Three to four short royal blue DNA segments on the lagging strand, each preceded by a short red RNA primer. Synthesized away from the fork.
callouts.description: Okazaki fragments are short segments of newly synthesized DNA on the lagging strand, each about 1,000–2,000 nucleotides long in prokaryotes (100–200 in eukaryotes). Each fragment begins with an RNA primer and is extended by DNA Pol III in the 5'→3' direction (away from the fork). After synthesis, the RNA primers are removed by DNA Pol I and replaced with DNA, and adjacent fragments are joined by DNA ligase to create a continuous strand.
callouts.ap_tip: Okazaki fragments are named after Reiji and Tsuneko Okazaki. The AP exam tests understanding of WHY they exist: because DNA Pol III can only synthesize 5'→3', and the lagging strand template is oriented so that synthesis must proceed away from the fork. Fragments are NOT caused by 'pausing' — they are an inherent consequence of antiparallel strand directionality.

callouts.label: DNA Polymerase I
callouts.hint: Medium purple oval enzyme on the lagging strand further from the fork, positioned where it is removing an RNA primer and replacing it with DNA.
callouts.description: DNA Polymerase I has a unique 5'→3' exonuclease activity that allows it to remove RNA primers one nucleotide at a time while simultaneously replacing them with DNA nucleotides. It works behind DNA Pol III on the lagging strand, processing older Okazaki fragments. After Pol I removes a primer and fills the gap with DNA, a small nick (break in the phosphodiester backbone) remains between adjacent fragments.
callouts.ap_tip: DNA Pol I has THREE enzymatic activities: 5'→3' polymerase, 3'→5' exonuclease (proofreading), and 5'→3' exonuclease (primer removal). The AP exam usually focuses on the primer removal function. Remember: Pol III does the bulk of replication; Pol I cleans up the primers.

callouts.label: DNA Ligase
callouts.hint: Small hot pink enzyme positioned at a nick between two completed Okazaki fragments, shown sealing the gap in the sugar-phosphate backbone.
callouts.description: DNA Ligase catalyzes the formation of a phosphodiester bond between the 3'-OH end of one Okazaki fragment and the 5'-phosphate end of the adjacent fragment, sealing the nick left after DNA Pol I replaces the RNA primer with DNA. This creates a continuous, unbroken sugar-phosphate backbone on the lagging strand. Ligase uses NAD+ (in prokaryotes) or ATP (in eukaryotes) as a cofactor for this reaction.
callouts.ap_tip: DNA Ligase seals NICKS (single-strand breaks in the backbone), NOT gaps. By the time ligase acts, Pol I has already filled in the DNA where the primer was. Ligase just forms the final covalent bond connecting adjacent nucleotides. The AP exam also tests ligase in the context of recombinant DNA technology — ligase joins DNA fragments in molecular cloning.
